A '''shrimp''' ({{plural form}}: shrimp ([[American English|US]]) or shrimps ([[British English|UK]])) is a [[common name]] typically used for [[crustacean]]s with an elongated body and a primarily [[Aquatic locomotion|swimming mode of locomotion]]. The name usually refers to [[decapod]]s belonging to the [[Caridea]] or [[Dendrobranchiata]], although some [[Shrimp#Non-decapods|crustaceans outside this order]] are also referred to as "shrimp". 

More narrow definitions may be restricted to Caridea, to smaller species of either of the aforementioned groups, or only the marine species. Under a broader definition, ''shrimp'' may be synonymous with [[prawn]], covering stalk-eyed swimming [[crustacean]]s with long, narrow muscular tails ([[Abdomen#Arthropoda|abdomens]]), long whiskers ([[Antenna (biology)|antennae]]), and slender, [[Biramous|biramous legs]].<ref>[http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/542046/shrimp Shrimp] ''Encyclopædia Britannica''. Retrieved 20 August 2012.</ref> They swim forward by paddling the [[swimmeret]]s on the underside of their abdomens, although their escape response is typically repeated flicks with the tail, driving them backwards very quickly ("[[Caridoid escape reaction|lobstering]]"). [[Crab]]s and [[lobster]]s have strong walking legs, whereas shrimp typically have thin, fragile legs which they use primarily for perching.<ref name=Rudloe1>Rudloe & Rudloe (2009), pp. 15–26.</ref>

Shrimp are widespread and abundant. There are thousands of species adapted to a wide range of habitats, both [[Fresh water|freshwater]] and marine; they can be found feeding near the [[seafloor]] on most coasts and estuaries, as well as in rivers and lakes. They play important roles in the [[food chain]] and are an important food source for larger animals ranging from fish to [[whale]]s; to [[Anti-predator adaptation|escape predators]], some species flip off the seafloor and dive into the sediment.<ref name=Rudloe1 /> They usually live from one to seven years.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nefsc.noaa.gov/faq/ |title=A bouillabaisse of fascinating facts about fish |publisher=[[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration|NOAA]]: [[National Marine Fisheries Service]] |access-date=October 22, 2009}}</ref> Shrimp are often solitary, though they can form large [[Shoaling and schooling|school]]s during the [[Seasonal breeder|spawning season]].<ref name=Rudloe1 /><ref name=Gracia1996>{{cite journal |author=A. Gracia |year=1996 |title=White shrimp (''Penaeus setiferus'') recruitment overfishing |journal=[[Marine and Freshwater Research]] |volume=47 |issue=1 |pages=59–65 |doi=10.1071/MF9960059 |bibcode=1996MFRes..47...59G }}</ref>

Being one of the more popular [[shellfish]] eaten, the muscular tails of many forms of shrimp are [[Shrimp and prawn as food|eaten by humans]], and they are widely [[Shrimp fishery|caught]] or [[Marine shrimp farming|farmed]] for human consumption. It is estimated that about 440 billion farmed shrimp, and about 25 trillion wild shrimp, are slaughtered annually.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Waldhorn |first1=Daniela |last2=Autric |first2=Elisa |date=11 August 2023 |title=Shrimp: The animals most commonly used and killed for food production  |url=https://rethinkpriorities.org/research-area/shrimp-the-animals-most-commonly-used-and-killed-for-food-production/#wild-caught-shrimp-estimates |website= |location= |publisher= |access-date=17 September 2026}}</ref> Excessive [[bycatch]] and [[overfishing]] (from wild shrimperies) is a significant concern, and waterbodies may suffer from [[Aquaculture#Issues|pollution]] when they are used to support shrimp farming.
